claims.text: A multi-scale ab initio framework can independently predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed framework will reduce overall prediction error by at least 30% relative to conventional models.
The relevant specimens are bulk, near-ideal HfNbTaTiZr samples prepared both without added oxygen and with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Combining DFT-informed interatomic potentials with separate electronic-transport corrections decouples lattice-vibrational and electronic heat-conduction mechanisms.
The framework is intended to apply from approximately 100 K to 1200 K.
Around 100 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Experimental thermal-conductivity data for the alloy are available up to 1200 K.
The framework should be validated for both defect-free material and oxygen-doped material.
Lattice thermal conductivity can be computed using ab initio molecular dynamics, Green–Kubo theory, and machine-learned force fields.
Electronic thermal conductivity can be computed separately using perturbative corrections to DFT electronic structures and Boltzmann transport calculations.
The dual lattice/electronic treatment avoids reliance on Debye-temperature approximations.
Earlier approaches use Debye-temperature assumptions or conflate lattice and electronic transport, causing inaccuracies when atomic-scale alloy complexity is important.
Separate predictions of lattice and electronic thermal conductivity will each agree with independent measurements within ±10%.
The approach will be robust for high-purity bulk refractory high-entropy alloys.
The approach may be less applicable to highly defective or nonhomogeneous samples.
Uncertainty will increase below 100 K because electron–phonon transport becomes more complex.
Electronic thermal conductivity can be inferred from electrical conductivity using Wiedemann–Franz and Lorenz-number analysis.
Phonon dispersion or spectroscopy can provide an independent measurement of lattice thermal conductivity.
Total thermal conductivity is the sum of electronic and lattice thermal conductivity.
The hypothesis is falsified if either component differs from measurement by more than ±10% or if error reduction relative to the baseline is less than 30%.
